analysis_sections.text: The reconstruction keeps the speaking face partly recognizable while spreading its appearance through coarse tonal bands. The original crop is still needed to inspect the actual mouth, eyes and head angle. This distinction is especially useful here: neither a blocky reconstruction nor a repeated attention region is a visible editing boundary. The spectral display supplies a transformed perspective that accompanies the signed readout and the explicit regional tests.
analysis_sections.title: A transformed view of the same face

analysis_sections.text: The signed maps show positive classifier support around central facial grid cells, with the strongest location changing between clips and pairs. In the first clip’s middle pair it is in the lower central grid; the second clip emphasizes a different upper-central location. These pair-specific readouts help explain the manipulated margin without requiring the attention selection to contain every positive patch or identifying a verified editing boundary.
analysis_sections.title: Where the classifier readout supports its decision

analysis_sections.text: The first proposal covers an eye and central-face area, while the second emphasizes the nose-bridge and central-face area. Each is produced by the explanation head and shared across the sampled frames of its clip. Repetition of a map therefore follows the display design. Its significance should be judged using the recorded regional experiments and perturbation checks rather than repeated appearance in the frame viewer.
analysis_sections.title: The explanation head’s proposed focus

analysis_sections.text: The regional checks provide a more limited result than the video classifier. In the first clip, the whole-curve comparisons do not favor the candidate over the strongest controls, even where an endpoint looks favorable. In the second, deletion increases the fake margin and a translation-overlap check fails. These results constrain the selected-region interpretation; they do not establish that the video classifier is wrong.

synthesis.headline: Detector strongly supports fake; visual candidate shows asymmetric lip and fold distortion during late head turn.
synthesis.summary: The detector provides strong support for manipulation. Visual inspection identifies a moderate-strength candidate: during the late head turn, the right mouth corner stretches disproportionately while the nasolabial fold vanishes and reappears without matching pose change.
synthesis.takeaway: A visible candidate warp in lip and fold behavior aligns with the detector’s strong fake classification, though no editing boundary is proven.

visual.summary: In the late head-turn window (case028/head-turn), the right mouth corner and upper lip show non-rigid distortion inconsistent with rigid rotation: the right lip stretches laterally while the left remains stable, and the nose-to-cheek transition shifts abruptly between frames 174–177 without corresponding head pose change.

windows.observed_change: From frame 171 to 177, the right mouth corner pulls outward and upward disproportionately relative to the left; the upper lip’s right side elongates while the left maintains curvature; the right nasolabial fold flattens abruptly at frame 174 then reappears by 177, despite minimal change in head yaw angle.
windows.ordinary_alternative: Motion blur plus slight expression change during rapid turn could cause apparent asymmetry, but fold disappearance/reappearance is atypical.
windows.why: Asymmetry in lip deformation exceeds expected projection effects; nasolabial fold discontinuity occurs without matching head rotation or expression shift.

windows.observed_change: From frame 24 to 48, mouth corners and upper lip deform smoothly with head yaw; nasolabial folds and cheek contours shift consistently with rigid rotation and gradual lip opening; no abrupt local distortions observed.
windows.ordinary_alternative: Standard perspective projection and articulation during speech and head movement.
windows.why: All facial feature changes scale uniformly with head orientation and articulation; no isolated region behaves independently of global motion.
